extracted.intended_audience: students and instructors of mathematical logic (undergraduate/graduate level)
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and constructive methods for representing wffs as Boolean functions, determining completeness of connective sets, converting formulas to normal forms, mapping formulas to switching circuits, and basic decidability/compactness results in propositional logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boolean function realized by a wff
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a wff α whose sentence symbols are among A1,...,An, define the n-place Boolean function Bn_α by Bn_α(X1,...,Xn) = the truth value given to α when A1,...,An are assigned X1,...,Xn (or equivalently v(α) where v is the truth-assignment with v(Ai)=Xi).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct Bα by evaluating α under each of the 2^n truth assignments for its sentence symbols and recording the resulting truth-value. Example: if α is A1 ∧ A2 then Bα(F,F)=F, Bα(F,T)=F, Bα(T,F)=F, Bα(T,T)=T. This formalizes moving from syntactic wffs to their semantic Boolean-function behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semantic consequence and equivalence via Boolean functions (Theorem 15A)
rubrics_metrics.description: For wffs α and β using sentence symbols among A1,...,An: (a) α |= β iff for all X ∈ {F,T}^n, Bα(X) ≤ Bβ(X) (with F < T). (b) α and β are tautologically equivalent (α |==| β) iff Bα = Bβ. (c) |= α iff Bα is the constant T function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pointwise comparison/equality of the Boolean functions realized by formulas to decide entailment, equivalence, and tautologicity. This reduces semantic questions about wffs to straightforward comparisons of truth tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every Boolean function is realizable by a wff (Post's theorem, Theorem 15B)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any n-place Boolean function G (n ≥ 1) there exists a wff α such that G = Bn_α; i.e., α realizes G.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct α by listing all n-tuples where G has value T and forming for each such tuple a conjunction γi that matches the tuple (use Aj if Xi_j = T, ¬Aj if Xi_j = F), then let α be the disjunction of those γi's. Example and full constructive proof provided in text. Special case: constant-F function realized by A1 ∧ ¬A1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disjunctive normal form existence (Corollary 15C)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any wff φ, there exists a tautologically equivalent wff α in disjunctive normal form (DNF): a disjunction γ1 ∨ ... ∨ γk where each γi is a conjunction of literals (sentence symbols or their negations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The DNF constructed in the proof of Post's theorem explicitly lists the satisfying truth-assignments. Advantage: DNF makes the satisfying assignments explicit. Note: the DNF produced may not be minimal; minimizing length leads to considerations of prime implicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness of connective sets ({∧,∨,¬}, {¬,∧}, {¬,∨})
rubrics_metrics.description: The set {∧, ∨, ¬} of connectives is complete: every Boolean function can be realized using only these connectives. Moreover, {¬, ∧} and {¬, ∨} are also complete (Theorem 15D).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given a formula using ∨, eliminate ∨ using De Morgan: β ∨ γ |==| ¬(¬β ∧ ¬γ). By induction (or repeated substitution) one can translate any formula into an equivalent one using only the desired subset. Completeness means the connective set suffices to express every Boolean function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method to show non-completeness (preservation of peculiarities)
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a set of connectives is not complete: prove (often by induction) that any wff built with those connectives has a certain preserved peculiarity, and then show some Boolean function lacks that peculiarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: {∧,→} is not complete because any formula using only these connectives with sentence symbol A assigned T yields T (i.e., α(T)=T), so nothing tautologically equivalent to ¬A can be formed. The method is to identify an invariant property of realizable functions and find a target function violating it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification and counting of connectives (0-,1-,2-,n-ary)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are 2^(2^n) distinct n-place Boolean functions; classify connectives by arity. 0-ary connectives correspond to constants (⊥, ⊤); unary connectives include identity and negation (only negation of real interest); among 16 binary connectives only 10 are 'really binary' (others collapse to unary or constant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the identification of connectives with their Boolean functions to catalog/connective behaviour. Table VI and the following text list common connectives (∧, ∨, →, ↔, exclusive-or, NAND, NOR, etc.) and note algebraic correspondences (e.g., ∧ as multiplication when F=0,T=1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-connective completeness (Sheffer stroke and NOR)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain single binary connectives are complete by themselves: the Sheffer stroke (NAND, '|') and NOR ('↓') each form a functionally complete set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show how ¬ and ∨ can be simulated with | or ↓ (e.g., ¬α |==| α | α and α ∨ β |==| (¬α) | (¬β) with suitable encodings). Since {¬, ∨} is complete, and these can simulate ¬ and ∨, they are complete alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of formulas as switching circuits; cost and delay optimization
rubrics_metrics.description: Map wffs to switching-circuit realizations where each connective corresponds to a device; define cost as number of devices used and delay (depth) as the maximum number of boxes a signal traverses from input to output. The engineering problem: given available devices and constraints (e.g., max delay), find an equivalent circuit of minimal cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circuits corresponding to tautologically equivalent wffs have identical truth-behaviour but may differ in cost and delay. Examples: majority-of-three implemented with two different circuits showing tradeoff in device count and same delay; minimizing cost subject to delay constraints is a central practical problem. Catalog of available devices determines the formal language of admissible formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recursive definition of formula/circuit delay
rubrics_metrics.description: Delay of a formula defined recursively: delay(sentence symbol)=0; delay(¬α)=delay(α)+1; delay(α ∧ β)=1+max(delay(α),delay(β)); similarly for other connectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this recursion to compute circuit depth corresponding to a formula. Examples compare delays of equivalent formulas to illustrate that syntactic transformations can increase device count and depth (e.g., (A1 ∧ A2) ∨ ¬A3 has delay 2, an equivalent ¬(A3 ∧ (¬A1 ∨ ¬A2)) has delay 4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicants, prime implicants, and minimal DNF (minimality criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A literal is a sentence symbol or its negation. An implicant of φ is a conjunction of distinct literals α such that α |= φ. A prime implicant is an implicant that ceases to be one upon deletion of any literal. Any minimal-length disjunction of implicants equivalent to φ must consist solely of prime implicants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To minimize a DNF representation, compute prime implicants and select a covering subcollection that yields φ. Exercises illustrate finding all prime implicants and possible minimal disjunctions. This is the logical basis of minimization algorithms (e.g., Quine–McCluskey, Karnaugh maps).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compactness theorem and finite-entailment corollary
rubrics_metrics.description: Compactness: a set Σ of wffs is satisfiable iff every finite subset of Σ is satisfiable. Corollary: If Σ |= τ then there exists a finite Σ0 ⊆ Σ with Σ0 |= τ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof strategy: extend a finitely satisfiable set to a maximally finitely satisfiable set (by recursive enumeration or Zorn's lemma), define a truth assignment v by membership in the maximal set, and show v satisfies the set. Use this corollary to reduce questions of entailment to finite cases (useful in decidability/enumerability arguments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of effective procedure and decidability notions
rubrics_metrics.description: An effective procedure is a finite, mechanical set of instructions executable by a diligent clerk or machine without ingenuity. A set of expressions is decidable if an effective procedure given ε decides (in finite time) whether ε is in the set. Semidecidable (semidecision) = there is a procedure that answers 'yes' iff ε ∈ A (may run forever otherwise). A set is effectively enumerable iff there exists a procedure that lists its members (every member appears eventually).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These informal definitions underlie theorems later made formal (recursive/recursively enumerable). Examples: The set of wffs is decidable (Theorem 17B) by a syntactic algorithm; the truth-table method gives decidability of finite entailment (Theorem 17C).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationships among decidability, semidecidability, and enumerability (Theorems 17E, 17F, 17G)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set A is effectively enumerable iff it is semidecidable (Theorem 17E). A set is decidable iff both it and its complement are effectively enumerable (Kleene's theorem, Theorem 17F). If Σ is decidable (or effectively enumerable), then the set of tautological consequences of Σ is effectively enumerable (Theorem 17G); for finite Σ, tautological consequences are decidable (Corollary 17D).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction methods: to enumerate a semidecidable set, dovetail tests over all expressions; to semidecide from an enumerator, watch the listing for membership. Use compactness to justify enumerability of tautological consequences by checking increasing finite subsets by truth tables.
